hld-notification:0.prompt: In a notification system that sends email, SMS and push, why do we usually put a message queue between the notification API and the channel senders?
options: Queues make each email deliver faster to the inbox
Queues decouple accepting a request from sending it, absorb bursts, and let each channel's workers scale and retry independently
Queues are required to call SMS provider APIs
Queues guarantee a user never receives a duplicate
hld-notification:0.explanation: The API can accept and persist a request quickly while channel workers drain queues at the rate providers allow, retrying failures without blocking callers. Queues do not make provider delivery faster and, being at-least-once, do not prevent duplicates on their own.

hld-notification:0.prompt: Why use a separate queue (or topic partition set) per channel rather than one shared queue for email, SMS and push?
options: Separate queues use less storage
Message brokers cannot mix message types in one queue
A slow or failing channel (e.g. an SMS provider outage) would otherwise back up the shared queue and delay the healthy channels
Push notifications must be encrypted differently
hld-notification:0.explanation: Per-channel queues isolate failures and let each channel scale to its provider's throughput (a bulkhead). Brokers can carry mixed messages; the problem with sharing is head-of-line blocking when one channel stalls.

hld-notification:0.prompt: A marketing campaign must notify 20 million users. What is the best way to fan this out?
options: The API loads all 20M users in memory and sends synchronously in one request
A database trigger sends each notification as rows are inserted
The client app polls for campaign messages every second
A job splits the audience into batches (e.g. by user-id range), enqueues batch tasks, and workers expand each batch into per-user channel messages
hld-notification:0.explanation: Batching the audience into tasks gives parallelism, checkpointing and the ability to resume after failures, while workers apply preferences and enqueue per channel. One giant synchronous request would time out and cannot resume partway.

hld-notification:0.prompt: For mobile push notifications, which service actually delivers the message to an iOS or Android device?
options: Your server opens a direct socket to each phone
The platform push services: APNs for iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for Android, using device tokens
The phone's SMS inbox
The app store servers
hld-notification:0.explanation: Your backend sends to APNs or FCM with the device token, and the platform keeps the persistent connection to the device. Servers do not hold sockets to every phone; app stores handle distribution, not messaging.

hld-notification:0.prompt: APNs/FCM respond that a device token is unregistered or invalid. What should the notification system do?
options: Retry the same token with exponential backoff for 24 hours
Mark the token invalid and remove it from the user's devices so future sends skip it
Fall back to sending the push via SMS
Ignore it; tokens recover automatically
hld-notification:0.explanation: An unregistered token means the app was uninstalled or the token rotated, so retrying is pointless and repeated sends to invalid tokens can hurt your sender reputation with the provider. Prune it and wait for the app to register a new token.

hld-notification:0.prompt: An order-confirmation notification and a weekly marketing digest compete for the same email workers. During a large campaign, confirmations are delayed by 40 minutes. What is the best fix?
options: Separate priority lanes: transactional messages get their own queue and reserved worker capacity ahead of bulk sends
Increase the email template cache size
Send confirmations by SMS instead
Lower the marketing campaign's batch size to 1
hld-notification:0.explanation: Transactional messages are time-sensitive and should never queue behind bulk; dedicated queues and capacity (often separate provider IP pools too) isolate them. Shrinking batch size only slows the campaign without guaranteeing priority.

hld-notification:0.prompt: Your email provider allows 500 sends/second for your account. A worker pool of 50 instances each sends as fast as possible. What should you add?
options: More worker instances to finish the queue faster
A global rate limiter (e.g. a shared token bucket) so the fleet's combined send rate stays under the provider's limit, with backoff on 429s
A per-instance limit of 500/second
A longer visibility timeout on the queue
hld-notification:0.explanation: The limit applies to the whole account, so the fleet needs a shared limiter; a per-instance 500/s across 50 instances allows 25,000/s. Adding workers just generates more 429 throttling errors.

hld-notification:0.prompt: Which details should a notification request carry from the producing service so the system can fan out correctly? Select all that apply.
options: Recipient user id (not raw contact details resolved by every caller)
Notification type or template id plus template variables
Priority or category (transactional vs marketing)
The SMTP server password
An idempotency key for the logical notification
hld-notification:0.explanation: Producers should send who, what (type + variables), how urgent and a dedup key; the notification service resolves contacts and preferences. Provider credentials must stay inside the notification service, never in request payloads.

hld-notification:0.prompt: The SMS provider has a full outage for 30 minutes. Which behaviours are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: Messages stay queued (or are retried with backoff) until the provider recovers or the message expires
Fail over to a secondary SMS provider if one is configured
Drop expired time-sensitive messages like OTPs rather than delivering them late
Block the email and push workers until SMS recovers
Retry each SMS in a tight loop with no delay
hld-notification:0.explanation: Queue/backoff, provider failover and TTL-based expiry handle an outage gracefully. Blocking other channels spreads the failure, and tight retry loops waste resources and can trigger more throttling when the provider returns.

hld-notification:0.prompt: A successful 202 response from an email provider's API means the email has landed in the recipient's inbox.
options: True
False
hld-notification:0.explanation: False. It means the provider accepted the message for delivery. Bounces, spam filtering and deferrals happen later and arrive via webhooks/events, which a notification system should ingest to track final status.

hld-notification:0.prompt: Storing every notification and its per-channel delivery status in a database (a notification log) is useful for auditing, debugging and showing an in-app notification history.
options: True
False
hld-notification:0.explanation: True. A notification log records what was requested, which channels were attempted and their outcomes. It supports support tickets, dedup checks and an in-app inbox; it needs retention/TTL policies because volume grows quickly.

hld-notification:1.prompt: Where should user notification preferences (e.g. 'no marketing SMS') be enforced?
options: In every producing service before it calls the notification system
In the mobile app, by hiding unwanted notifications
Centrally in the notification service before messages are enqueued to channels
Only at the email provider via unsubscribe lists
hld-notification:1.explanation: Central enforcement means one consistent rule set and no producer can forget to check. Hiding on the device still sends (and bills for) the message, and provider-level lists cover only one channel.

hld-notification:1.prompt: Which preference model is the most practical for a notification system?
options: One global on/off switch per user
Per-user settings by category and channel (e.g. 'order updates: push+email; marketing: email only'), with sensible defaults
A free-text field the user fills in
Preferences per individual notification template id only
hld-notification:1.explanation: Category × channel matches how users think ('I want order updates, not promos') and stays manageable as templates grow. A single switch is too coarse; per-template settings explode in number and confuse users.

hld-notification:1.prompt: A user has opted out of all notifications. A password-reset email is triggered. What should happen?
options: Send it: security and account-critical transactional messages typically bypass marketing opt-outs
Drop it, because opt-out applies to every message
Send it by SMS instead
Queue it until the user opts back in
hld-notification:1.explanation: Required transactional messages (password resets, security alerts, receipts) are normally exempt from marketing opt-outs because the user explicitly requested them or they are essential. Dropping it would lock the user out.

hld-notification:1.prompt: Users complain about getting 15 push notifications in an hour when many people like their post. What is the best design change?
options: Disable push for likes entirely
Send each like as an SMS instead
Increase the push provider's rate limit
Per-user frequency caps plus batching/digesting: collapse events within a window into one notification like 'Alex and 14 others liked your post'
hld-notification:1.explanation: Caps and aggregation keep the signal while cutting noise. Raising provider limits makes the spam worse, and disabling the category removes value users may want.

hld-notification:1.prompt: How would you implement a rule like 'at most 3 marketing pushes per user per day' at high scale?
options: Count rows in the notification log with a SQL COUNT for every send
A per-user counter in Redis keyed by user and day (INCR with an expiry), checked before enqueueing
Keep counters in each worker's memory
Ask the push provider to enforce it
hld-notification:1.explanation: A Redis INCR on a key like cap:{user}:{date} with a TTL is atomic, fast and shared by all workers. Counting log rows per send is expensive at scale, and in-memory counters are wrong when several workers serve the same user.

hld-notification:1.prompt: Quiet hours say 'no non-urgent notifications between 22:00 and 08:00'. Where does a common bug come from?
options: Using the user's local time zone instead of UTC
Storing quiet hours as two integers
Evaluating the window in server time or UTC instead of the user's time zone, and mishandling windows that cross midnight
Applying quiet hours to marketing messages
hld-notification:1.explanation: Quiet hours are local to the user, so the check must convert to the user's time zone, and 22:00–08:00 crosses midnight so start > end must be handled. Using the user's zone is the fix, not the bug.

hld-notification:1.prompt: During quiet hours, a non-urgent notification arrives. Which handling is usually best?
options: Drop it permanently
Send it immediately but silently via SMS
Delay it: schedule delivery for when quiet hours end (or fold it into a morning digest), unless it expires first
Send it via email at 3 a.m.
hld-notification:1.explanation: Deferring respects the user while preserving the message; expiry rules drop things that would be stale by morning. Dropping loses value, and switching channels to bypass quiet hours violates the intent.

hld-notification:1.prompt: Which inputs should the preference/rate-limit check consider before a message is enqueued? Select all that apply.
options: The user's channel and category opt-ins
Frequency caps already used today
Quiet hours in the user's time zone
Legal unsubscribe/suppression lists (e.g. hard-bounced emails, STOP replies)
The CPU usage of the push provider
hld-notification:1.explanation: Preferences, caps, quiet hours and suppression lists all decide whether to send. Provider CPU usage is not visible or relevant; provider throttling is handled by the senders' rate limiting and retries.

hld-notification:1.prompt: Preferences are read on every notification (tens of thousands per second). Which designs keep this fast and correct? Select all that apply.
options: Cache preferences (e.g. Redis or in-process with short TTL) and invalidate on update
Batch-load preferences for a whole audience chunk during campaign fan-out
Store preferences only in the client app and ask it each time
Fall back to the safest default (don't send marketing) if preferences cannot be loaded
Read from the primary database with a full table scan per message
hld-notification:1.explanation: Caching with invalidation and batch loads cut database load, and a fail-safe default avoids spamming opted-out users when the store is down. Asking devices or scanning tables per message does not scale.

hld-notification:1.prompt: Frequency caps should usually apply to transactional messages like OTP codes the same way they apply to marketing messages.
options: True
False
hld-notification:1.explanation: False. Capping OTPs or receipts would break core flows. Transactional messages need separate, abuse-oriented limits (e.g. max OTP requests per phone per hour) rather than marketing-style engagement caps.

hld-notification:1.prompt: When a user replies STOP to an SMS, the system should add the number to a suppression list and stop sending non-required SMS to it, even if the in-app preference still shows SMS enabled.
options: True
False
hld-notification:1.explanation: True. Carrier-level opt-outs (and laws like TCPA in the US) must be honoured; the suppression list overrides app settings, and ideally the app preference is updated to match so the two stay consistent.

hld-notification:2.prompt: Why can a notification be sent twice even with a reliable queue?
options: Queues randomly duplicate messages
Most queues deliver at least once: a worker may send the message and crash (or time out) before acknowledging, so it is redelivered
Email providers always send two copies
Push tokens are duplicated per device
hld-notification:2.explanation: At-least-once delivery means an un-acked message comes back. If the side effect (sending) happened before the ack, it repeats. Deduplication or idempotency is needed on top of the queue.

hld-notification:2.prompt: Which key is the best choice for deduplicating notification sends?
options: The current timestamp in milliseconds
A random UUID generated by the worker on each attempt
The user's email address alone
A deterministic idempotency key for the logical notification, e.g. hash(event id, user id, channel)
hld-notification:2.explanation: The key must be the same across retries of the same logical message and different for distinct messages. A per-attempt UUID or timestamp changes on retry, and email alone would block every future notification to that user.

hld-notification:2.prompt: A worker checks Redis for the dedup key, finds nothing, sends the email, then sets the key. Two workers process the same redelivered message concurrently. What happens?
options: Both may pass the check before either sets the key, so the email is sent twice
Redis serialises the GET and SET so only one sends
The second worker gets an error from the email provider
The queue prevents concurrent delivery of the same message
hld-notification:2.explanation: Check-then-act is a race. Claim the key atomically first, e.g. SET key value NX EX ttl, and only the worker that wins the claim sends. Separate GET and SET calls are not atomic in Redis, and queues can redeliver while the first attempt is still running.

hld-notification:2.prompt: A worker atomically claims the dedup key (SET NX) and then crashes before sending. The message is redelivered. What is the consequence, and the common mitigation?
options: The email is sent twice; mitigation is to remove dedup
The redelivered message sees the claimed key and is skipped, so nothing is sent; mitigate by storing a status (claimed vs sent) with a short claim TTL so stale claims can be retried
Redis rolls back the key automatically when the worker dies
The queue detects the crash and sends the email itself
hld-notification:2.explanation: Claiming before acting trades duplicates for possible loss. Recording claimed/sent states with a short claim lease lets a retry take over an expired claim. Redis does not roll back keys when a client dies.

hld-notification:2.prompt: Which retry policy fits sending to an external SMS provider that intermittently returns 503?
options: Retry immediately in a loop until it succeeds
Never retry; drop the message on the first failure
Retry on a fixed 1-second interval forever
Bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, then move the message to a dead-letter queue
hld-notification:2.explanation: Backoff with jitter avoids hammering a struggling provider, a retry cap stops infinite loops, and a DLQ keeps failed messages for inspection or replay. Immediate loops worsen overload; no retries loses messages on transient errors.

hld-notification:2.prompt: What is a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for in a notification pipeline?
options: Holding messages that exhausted their retries or are malformed, so they stop blocking the main queue and can be inspected or replayed
Storing notifications for users who have died
Holding low-priority marketing messages
Caching successful sends for deduplication
hld-notification:2.explanation: A DLQ isolates poison or repeatedly failing messages so the main queue keeps flowing, and gives operators a place to debug and replay. It is not a priority lane or a dedup store.

hld-notification:2.prompt: An OTP SMS fails and is retried with backoff. The 4th retry would happen 9 minutes after the request, but the OTP expires after 5 minutes. What should the design include?
options: Longer OTP validity to match the retry schedule
A message TTL/expiry: drop (and record) the send once it is past its useful lifetime
More retries so delivery eventually succeeds
Switch the OTP to email automatically after each failure
hld-notification:2.explanation: Time-sensitive messages need an expiry checked before each attempt; delivering a dead OTP only confuses the user. Weakening OTP security to fit retries is backwards.

hld-notification:2.prompt: Which events should a notification system ingest from providers to keep delivery state accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Email bounce and complaint (spam report) webhooks
SMS delivery receipts (delivered/failed)
Push provider responses indicating invalid tokens
The provider's internal deployment schedule
Unsubscribe events from list-unsubscribe links
hld-notification:2.explanation: Bounces, complaints, delivery receipts, invalid tokens and unsubscribes update status and suppression lists so you stop sending to bad addresses. Provider deployment schedules are irrelevant to per-message state.

hld-notification:2.prompt: An upstream service publishes the same 'OrderShipped' event twice (its own at-least-once delivery). Which measures stop the user getting two shipping notifications? Select all that apply.
options: Derive the idempotency key from the upstream event id, not from the time the notification service received it
Keep a record of processed event ids for a retention window and skip repeats
Use a unique constraint on (event_id, user_id, channel) in the notification log
Process events with more consumer instances
Rely on the email provider to drop duplicates
hld-notification:2.explanation: Dedup must key on the upstream event's identity and be enforced atomically (processed-id store or unique constraint). More consumers do not dedupe, and providers generally do not deduplicate your sends.

hld-notification:2.prompt: If the notification service deduplicates by idempotency key, it can safely use at-least-once delivery from its queue.
options: True
False
hld-notification:2.explanation: True. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives effectively-once outcomes, the standard practical design. Exactly-once delivery across a queue and an external provider is not achievable on its own.

hld-notification:2.prompt: A hard email bounce (e.g. 'mailbox does not exist') should be retried with exponential backoff just like a temporary failure.
options: True
False
hld-notification:2.explanation: False. Hard bounces are permanent: add the address to the suppression list and stop. Repeatedly sending to invalid addresses damages sender reputation. Soft bounces (mailbox full, temporary deferral) are the ones to retry.

hld-notification:3.prompt: Why store notification templates in a template service/store instead of hard-coding message text in each producing service?
options: Templates make sending cheaper per message
Hard-coded strings cannot contain variables
Message copy, localisation and per-channel formats can change without redeploying producers, and stay consistent across services
Template stores are required by email providers
hld-notification:3.explanation: Centralised templates let product/marketing edit copy, add languages and adjust channel formats while producers just send a template id plus variables. Hard-coded strings can use variables, but changing them needs code deploys in many services.

hld-notification:3.prompt: A template renders user-supplied data like a display name into HTML email. What is the main security concern?
options: The email may be too long
Injection: unescaped user input can inject HTML/links (phishing) into emails sent by your trusted domain
The template engine may run out of memory
Recipients may not have HTML email enabled
hld-notification:3.explanation: If variables are inserted unescaped, a malicious display name can add links or markup that appear to come from you. Use a template engine with auto-escaping for HTML and sanitise or restrict any intentionally raw content.

hld-notification:3.prompt: A template team edits the 'order shipped' template while a campaign is mid-send. Some users receive the old text, some the new. How do you avoid this kind of inconsistency?
options: Lock the template table during every campaign
Render all messages before sending any of them
Store templates only in the application code
Version templates immutably and pin each send (or campaign) to a specific template version
hld-notification:3.explanation: Immutable versions mean edits create a new version; in-flight sends keep the version they were enqueued with, and you can roll back. Table locks block editing, and pre-rendering millions of messages wastes storage and still does not version anything.

hld-notification:3.prompt: One logical notification ('Your order shipped') must go out via email, SMS and push. How should templates be modelled?
options: One template per notification type with a channel-specific variant for each channel (rich HTML email, short SMS, title+body push)
A single HTML template, stripped of tags for SMS and push
A separate notification type per channel, unrelated to each other
Only email gets a template; SMS and push reuse the email subject
hld-notification:3.explanation: Channels have very different constraints (SMS length/encoding, push title/body limits, HTML email), so each needs its own variant under one notification type that shares variables. Auto-stripping HTML produces poor, often over-long SMS.

hld-notification:3.prompt: How should localisation be handled for templates?
options: Translate messages at send time with a machine-translation API for every message
Store per-locale variants of each template and pick by the user's locale, falling back to a default locale when missing
Send all messages in English and let the device translate
Create a separate notification type for each country
hld-notification:3.explanation: Per-locale variants with fallback give reviewed, consistent copy and predictable behaviour. Per-send machine translation adds latency, cost and quality risk, and separate notification types per country duplicate everything else.

hld-notification:3.prompt: An SMS template with an emoji suddenly makes each message cost 3x more. What is the most likely reason?
options: Emoji require MMS instead of SMS on all carriers
The template engine doubled the variables
The emoji forces UCS-2 encoding, cutting the per-segment limit from 160 to 70 characters, so the message splits into more billable segments
Carriers charge a fixed emoji surcharge
hld-notification:3.explanation: SMS uses GSM-7 (160 chars/segment) unless a character falls outside it; then the whole message uses UCS-2 at 70 chars/segment (67 when concatenated), so a 150-char message becomes 3 segments. It still goes as SMS, not MMS.

hld-notification:3.prompt: A producer sends template variables that do not include `firstName`, which the template uses. What is the most robust behaviour?
options: Validate variables against the template's declared schema at request time and reject (or apply a defined default) before enqueueing
Render 'Hi undefined,' and send anyway
Silently drop the message at render time
Let the email provider fill in a placeholder
hld-notification:3.explanation: Declaring each template's variables and validating at the API boundary catches producer bugs early with a clear error, or applies an intentional fallback like 'Hi there'. Rendering 'undefined' ships a broken message; silent drops hide the bug.

hld-notification:3.prompt: Which features are valuable in a template management system? Select all that apply.
options: Preview/test rendering with sample variables before publishing
Version history and rollback
Per-channel and per-locale variants
Arbitrary code execution inside templates for flexibility
A declared list of required variables per template
hld-notification:3.explanation: Previews, versioning, variants and variable schemas make templates safe to edit. Allowing arbitrary code in templates edited by non-engineers creates security (server-side template injection) and reliability risks; use a logic-less or sandboxed engine.

hld-notification:3.prompt: Rendering is a hot path at 50k messages/second. Which optimisations are sensible? Select all that apply.
options: Cache compiled templates in memory keyed by template id + version
Render in the channel workers close to sending, rather than in the API request path
Re-fetch and re-compile the template from the database for every message
Batch-load recipient data needed for variables during campaign fan-out
Because versions are immutable, cache them without needing invalidation
hld-notification:3.explanation: Compiling once and caching by immutable version (so no invalidation is needed), rendering in workers and batch-loading data keep rendering cheap. Fetching and compiling per message wastes database and CPU at this rate.

hld-notification:3.prompt: Push notification payloads have size limits (e.g. 4 KB on APNs and FCM), so push templates should keep the payload small and link to details in the app.
options: True
False
hld-notification:3.explanation: True. APNs and FCM cap payloads at about 4 KB, and lock screens truncate long text anyway. Send a short title/body plus an id or deep link so the app fetches full details.

hld-notification:3.prompt: Template rendering should happen in the producing service so the notification service only forwards finished text.
options: True
False
hld-notification:3.explanation: False. Rendering centrally means the notification service can apply locale, channel variant and template version consistently after preference checks. If producers render, every service duplicates template logic and copy changes need redeploys.
